extraction_text: The Mahabharata is a compilation of discourses from religious thinkers during the epic period, reflecting a society of intellectual contention similar to China's 'Hundred Schools of Thought' era.
According to epic mythology, the universe undergoes endless cycles of creation and destruction under divine manipulation.
At the beginning of creation, the world is submerged in water, with Vishnu lying on the surface; Brahma awakens from a lotus growing from Vishnu's navel and creates all beings.
After a thousand ages, at the end of a cosmic cycle, the universe is destroyed by drought, wind, fire, and flood, with Brahma falling asleep in the lotus before a new creation begins.
Due to oral transmission, variations exist in myths, such as Brahma awakening from a golden egg instead of a lotus, both accepted in the Mahabharata.
In the Shanti Parva Chapter 335, it's synthesized that Brahma is born from Vishnu's thought in the first creation, and from his eye, speech, ear, nose, golden egg, and lotus in subsequent ones.
A cosmic cycle lasts a thousand ages, during which human society cycles through the Satya Yuga, Treta Yuga, Dvapara Yuga, and Kali Yuga, each marked by declining dharma.
In the Kali Yuga, when dharma is minimal, Vishnu incarnates as the Brahmin Kalki to destroy evil, restore dharma, and re-establish the Satya Yuga.
Describes the durations of four cosmic ages: Satya Yuga (4,800 years), Treta Yuga (3,600 years), Dvapara Yuga (2,400 years), and Kali Yuga (1,200 years).

The Narayana doctrine venerates Narayana, Vishnu, or Vasudeva's son (Krishna) as the principal deity of the Pancharatra sect.
A Brahmin seeks a deity who is not indifferent to human prayers and finds such a deity in the water-pot cloud.

attributes.result: Discovery of deity in water-pot cloud

extraction_text: Two lifestyles are discussed: the path of action (fulfilling duties in four life stages) and the path of renunciation (abandoning worldly life, living on alms).
In a father-son dialogue, the son and Shuka in his inquiry to Vyasa argue that one who has attained true knowledge should renounce the world and seek self-knowledge.
Shamikeya praises the ideal of having nothing as the greatest happiness and extols the wandering ascetic's life.
Harita also praises the renouncer's ideal of kindness to all beings, non-harm, and begging for food at appropriate times.

attributes.action: Endorsement of renunciation with specific practices

extraction_text: Shuka is presented as a representative of the renunciation path.
Sumalashimi is one of the most ardent advocates of the householder's life.
Vyasa and Parashara affirm that only householder life ensures the continuation of the human race and supports other life stages.
Parashara explains the importance of householder life for repaying debts to gods, ancestors, and guests.
Parashara and the swan-formed Prajapati declare no honor greater than being born human, even as the lowest.
The conflict between action and renunciation paths is resolved through the lifestyles of Janaka and Durlabharaya.
The text discusses the ethical teachings in the 'Mokshadharma Parva' (Liberation Law Section) of the Mahabharata, emphasizing detachment and renunciation.

attributes.relationships: General ethical principles for all individuals

extraction_text: The text mentions Janaka and Durlabha as examples of individuals who practice action while maintaining detachment.

attributes.relationships: Examples of practitioners of detachment

extraction_text: The text highlights the importance of 'Mounins' (silent reciters) and 'Uñchavrittis' (gleaners) as ethical teachers in the Mokshadharma Parva.

attributes.relationships: Ethical teachers/role models

attributes.relationships: Critics of ritual animal sacrifice

attributes.relationships: Shift in ritual practice

attributes.relationships: Critic of capital punishment

attributes.relationships: Teacher of non-violence

attributes.relationships: General social ethics

extraction_text: Discussion of various atonement methods (Chapters 35-36) and discussion of permissible and impermissible foods (Chapter 37) are inserted.
More questions about royal law or king's duties (from 12.38.1 onward) are raised, forming the main topics of the Rajadharma Parva.
Duties during times of crisis form the topic of the next section, the Apaddharma Parva.
The discussion of atonement methods is noted as not entirely fitting the immediate topic and appears elsewhere in this section and in the later-added Anushasana Parva.
Most manuscripts incorrectly show Krishna personally sprinkling consecration water.
It is noted that among the 101 names, Narayana is not included.
Bhishma's meditation is called the Bhishma-stava-raja (12.47.10-63), containing 32 verses in this version but 108 names in popular versions due to 108 being a sacred number.

During the first day's journey from the capital to the battlefield, passing by Rama's lake (a river filled with Kshatriya blood), Krishna narrates how Parashurama previously exterminated Kshatriyas from the earth.
Hastinapura is located on the Ganges, and Kurukshetra is near the Drishadvati and Sarasvati rivers, where Bhishma lies on his 'bed of arrows'.

The distance between them is about 100 yojanas, and listeners typically travel back and forth daily, as seen from 12.52.30-33 where at the end of the first day's talk, the sun sets and listeners rise to return.
In Maithili and Bengali manuscripts and several Southern manuscripts, two parts are merged into one.
For example, in 12.60.36-38, manuscripts differ on whether Shudras can participate in sacrifices.
Twice-born refers to Brahmins, who begin a second life at the age of Veda study. Birds are oviparous and also called twice-born.
